copy.headline: Boston's waterways are its widest empty highway.
copy.subline: A zero-emission, electric-foiling commuter network on Boston Harbor — built on existing piers, financed by private capital, aligned with the Commonwealth's own water-transportation plans.

copy.lead: Massachusetts is already asking this question. The state's own Water Transportation Study frames ferries as "convenient transit in communities with limited public transportation options" and a resilience layer "when there are disruptions to subway or Commuter Rail service."
copy.support: The same study is actively scoping new routes and terminals in Boston, Lynn, Quincy, Salem, and Winthrop — five of the eighteen stations on this network.

copy.headline: Any sound pier or marina berth is a station. No terminals to build.
copy.body: Zero terminal capital cost for the city or state. Service can start at existing public piers and municipal marinas — the landings on this network are already built.

landings_verified.note: per-stop verification status intentionally omitted from this page (fail closed)

operate_proof_points.proof: Owns vessels, funds routes, and directly procures operating contracts across nine ferry routes — the clearest public vessel-operator precedent in this market.
Funds and manages the Seaport Ferry (Lovejoy Wharf–Fan Pier–East Boston), launched on a pilot basis.

copy.enable_track: Grant landing access at existing public piers and a permitting pathway for a pilot corridor. Private capital finances the fleet; privately committed employer demand fills the seats. The ask is access, not money.
copy.operate_track: Massachusetts public bodies already own and operate ferry fleets. Navier vessels can be procured the way transit vehicles are procured — to build, run, or augment the public water network.
copy.framing: Two ways to partner — a genuine choice, not a pitch fork. Boston's landscape leans Enable, with proven public operators alongside.

pillars: Zero-emission electric foiling — direct alignment with Boston's transportation-electrification goals.
Minimal wake foilborne and near-silent at speed — relevant to shoreline permitting and harbor neighbors.
Quality of life: waterfront activation, commute time returned to residents, and a business-attraction asset for waterfront districts.

stats.stat: MBTA ferry ridership: 1,498,200 riders in 2025 (~2,700/weekday, Q1 2026)
stats.note: evidence Massachusetts commuters already value and use water transit

stats.stat: MBTA ferries post the highest on-time performance and farebox recovery of any MBTA mode
$2.3M in state awards (Aug 2025) to expand ferry and water transportation on Boston Harbor, including $1M to redesign the Winthrop/Quincy route and triple daily capacity

copy.headline: Your speed rules were written for boats that make wake.
copy.body: Harbor speed rules exist to control wake, wash, noise, and disturbance. Massachusetts law already draws the right distinction: 323 CMR 2 separately prohibits harmful wash — an outcome a foiling Navier satisfies inherently — while capping headway speed at 6 mph in regulated situations. The regulations even contain an existing relief mechanism: marked-channel permission granted by an authorized marine-enforcement agency.
copy.invitation: Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows the rule's purpose is served, grant route-specific relief through the mechanism your own regulations already provide.
copy.precedent: Precedent exists: on Region Stockholm's Route 89, a Candela P-12 electric hydrofoil operated at ~22 knots in a ~12-knot zone under a low-wake speed exemption (attributed to Länsstyrelsen, the county administrative board).

rule_basis.detail: headway speed defined as minimum steerage speed, not over 6 mph

prohibits wash thrown into other vessels/floats; requires headway speed near marinas/floats/swimmers and in channels unless an authorized marine-enforcement agency permits otherwise with marked speeds

data.base_times_policy: All map and trip times on this page respect posted limits. No exemption is assumed. Relief renders only in the labeled 'what relief unlocks' layer, which for Boston carries no numbers this pass.

plans.plan: MassDOT Water Transportation Study (Summer 2025 – Summer 2026, in progress)
plans.quote: convenient transit in communities with limited public transportation options
plans.quote2: when there are disruptions to subway or Commuter Rail service
plans.alignment: The study is actively scoping new routes/terminals in Boston, Lynn, Quincy, Salem, and Winthrop — five stations on this network.
Carbon-neutral-by-2050 goal with emissions cut in half by 2030; an all-electric hydrofoil network materially advances the transportation-electrification pillar.
The state has already put new money behind the North Shore, South Shore, and Quincy corridors this network serves, including tripling Winthrop/Quincy ferry capacity.

copy.intro: Boston Harbor's water-transportation landscape spans state, regional, and municipal bodies. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: Runs nine public ferry routes; owns vessels and procures operating contracts — the region's proven public water-transit operator.
State transportation secretariat; leads the cross-agency Water Transportation Study (Summer 2025–Summer 2026) scoping five stations on this network.
Funds and manages the Seaport Ferry serving Fan Pier and Lovejoy Wharf.
Waterfront planning and Municipal Harbor Plans for the South Boston, Downtown, and East Boston waterfronts.
Port authority and underlying landowner at Commonwealth Pier; grants landing access at existing public docks.
Public-trust licensing for tideland structures; existing landings used as-is generally need no new license — modifications do.
Landowner at Squantum Point Park (Quincy) and the Hingham ferry terminal, which the MBTA operates under long-term lease.
State-chartered body coordinating port development within Salem Harbor, including Salem Wharf.

bodies.body: Harbor towns and cities — Hull, Winthrop, Quincy, Hingham
bodies.role: Own or co-manage their municipal landings (Pemberton Point, Winthrop Town Landing, Squantum Point partnership, Hewitts Cove harbor operations).
Steward of part of Charlestown Navy Yard; carries a federal mandate to improve Boston Harbor Islands access through public water transportation.
